sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No. Every percentage appears twice. The pie labels all 14 slices: four in white inside the large wedges, and ten small ones (4%, 3% ×4, 2% ×4, 1%) on leader lines fanned around the upper left (roughly x 80–310, y 215–410). The legend at the right then gives all 14 values again in a bold column (x ≈ 1025–1060, y 225–650). The reader finds each number twice. The ten small outside labels with their tick marks crowd the left of the pie and are the busiest part of the page, yet they add nothing the legend lacks. They are also harder to tie to a category, because the reader still has to match each one to the legend by colour. Source: Nielsen heuristic 8 (aesthetic and minimalist design); Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 4, on ink that carries no new information. Fix: make one place carry the numbers. Either drop the outside labels and let the legend hold all the values, or put the category names on the chart and drop the legend. The chart-form question (14 slices in a pie) belongs to the data section. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No, weakly. "Where operating costs went in fiscal 2026" names the topic, and the deck repeats it ("Share of total operating costs by category…"). Neither line says what the chart shows. The reader has to work out the point alone, for example that staff costs are 38% and the top four categories make up three quarters of the total, while the other ten together come to about a quarter. In an annual report, a headline or deck that states the finding gives the chart something to prove. Fix: keep the section label, and make the deck or headline state the main fact in the reader's terms. The chart then backs up that sentence instead of standing alone. The entry's source is not on the approved list, so this is my own judgment. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The page reads as one whole. It uses one serif for the headline and deck, one sans for labels and the legend, a warm off-white ground, and a muted, earthy palette with no hue that shouts. The tone suits a sober annual report, and the page feels like part of a set ("Section 4 of 9").
- The copy is finished and checks out. The 14 shares add up to exactly 100. The source line states the fiscal year and that the figures are rounded. The section label "4.2 Costs" and the headline say exactly what the page holds.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (every element does a job; image and headline make one idea), 0 unsure

Walk (working notes):

First read: the eye lands on the bold serif headline "Where operating costs went in fiscal 2026", then drops to the dark-blue 38% slice. It reads as a chart page from a company annual report. It feels calm and sober. Image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

What matters first:
- One element dominates: **yes.** The headline (~32 px bold serif, near-black) leads, and the 38% slice is the clear focal point of the chart.
- Distinct text levels, no near-equal sizes: **yes.** Eyebrow (small caps, brown) → title (large bold serif) → subtitle (regular grey serif, ~17 px) → legend (sans, ~15 px) → source (~12 px grey). The ~14 px header and ~15 px legend are close in size, but they sit in separate zones and have different jobs, so they don't compete.
- Headings differ in more than size: **yes.** The title is bold serif in near-black. The subtitle is regular-weight serif in grey. The eyebrow is tracked caps in a colour.

No line answered `no` or `unsure`, so I had no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The headline leads, and the chart leads within its own area.** The large bold serif title (y≈105–140) is the clear place to start. In the chart, the 38% Salaries slice is the biggest, darkest shape and carries the largest white label. So the eye gets the main point (most of the money goes on people) right after the title, with no searching. Keep the title and the slice as the only two heavy things on the page.
- **Each heading level differs in more than size.** The eyebrow "4.2 COSTS" is small, tracked caps in a muted brown. The title is a bold serif in near-black. The subtitle is the same serif at regular weight in grey. Each step down drops in weight or colour as well as size, so the levels separate at a glance without needing more font sizes.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** No. The page sets up a text column from x≈64 to x≈1216: the left edge is shared by the header, the "4.2 COSTS" kicker, the title, the subtitle and the source line, and "Annual report 2026 · Section 4 of 9" ends at about 1216. The chart band doesn't use that right edge. The legend's rules and its right-aligned % column stop at about x≈1060, which lines up with nothing above or below. The pie and the legend also split the band at about 64–515 and 620–1060, which looks like a split made by eye rather than columns taken from the page.
   - **What the viewer sees:** a strip about 156 px wide (x 1060–1216, y ≈220–660) sits empty next to the legend's numbers. The figure looks pushed left and a little short of the frame the header and title set. The percentages, which are what the reader looks up, end in mid-air instead of on the page's right margin.
   - **Why:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, and Samara, *Making and Breaking the Grid*: a block whose edges match no other block shows that it was placed by eye.
   - **Fix:** take the chart band's edges from the page grid. One way is to run the legend's right edge, rules and % column to the 1216 margin and widen the gap to match. Another is to set the pie and legend on two named columns that also govern the header and title (for example, halves of 64–1216).
   - Convention. Minor: it costs polish and a sense of finish, not understanding.

**What's working.**
- One strong left edge at x≈64 carries the header, kicker, title, subtitle and source down the page. The page reads as one ordered column, and the eye drops straight from the headline into the chart.
- The spacing groups things correctly. Kicker, title and subtitle sit tight as one unit, there's a clear gap before the chart, and the legend's rows are spaced much closer than the gap between pie and legend. Each group reads as one at a glance, with no stray elements.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (all blocks on one grid)

The page's type is well set. The only failure is that two of the white percentage labels inside the pie are too low in contrast; the legend repeats both numbers, so nothing is lost.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Does text on a plain background reach 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text), placeholder and helper text included?"**: no.
   - **Where:** the white percentage labels inside the pie. "12%" sits on the orange slice (about x 220–257, y 528–547) and "16%" on the teal slice (about x 327–364, y 548–567).
   - **What the viewer meets:** the labels look about 17 px bold, just under the 18.66 px bold that counts as large text, so they need 4.5:1. By eye, white on that orange is about 2.7:1 and white on that teal about 3.2:1. That puts both in the 2.5 to 4.4 band, where text reads as faint. "9%" on the purple is borderline, about 4.5:1. "38%" on the dark blue is fine. These are the second and third biggest costs, the numbers a reader is most likely to quote, and they are the hardest on the page to read for anyone with low vision or on a projector.
   - **Why:** WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3.
   - **Fix:** darken the text or change its background until each label reaches at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 if it is made large text. For example, use dark text on the light slices (orange, teal) and keep white on the dark ones. Or deepen those two fills. Or set the labels at 19 px bold or more.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, minor. The legend at the right repeats each value in dark bold type, so nothing is lost; it only slows the reader.

**What's working.**
- **The type plan:** a bold serif headline and a lighter serif subtitle sit over a plain sans for the legend, labels and source line. That gives three clear levels with nothing extra. The headline is set tight with a real "fi" ligature in "fiscal". The small-caps kicker "4.2 COSTS" is letterspaced as capitals should be.
- **The legend figures:** they are bold and right-aligned in one column (38% down to 1%), so they scan as a ranked list and the eye can compare shares without going back to the slices.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (text contrast 4.5:1: white "12%" and "16%" on the orange and teal slices).

**Walk (working notes, Color).** Bash was refused, so I couldn't run the crop script and worked from the whole image (1280×800, about one screen). This section covers colour outside charts, so I'm leaving the pie and legend colours to the data critic.
1. Small palette: yes. Warm off-white ground, near-black and grey text, and one muted brown accent on the "4.2 COSTS" eyebrow.
2. Saturated colour kept small: yes. Outside the chart everything is neutral.
3. Light-to-dark range: yes. The dark serif title and body sit on a light ground, and the header rule is faint but structural.
4. Warm forward, cool back: yes. The only warm accent is the eyebrow, and that is fine.
5. Matching colours look the same: yes.
6. No vibrating edges: yes, outside the chart.
7. Status colours: yes, outside the chart. The red and green category slices are a chart matter.
8. Colour not alone: yes, outside the chart.
9. Dark theme: yes (not a dark theme).

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The surface outside the chart is only page chrome and type, so almost everything that matters about colour here sits inside the chart and belongs to the data section. For the data critic, from this pass:
- 14 categorical hues.
- Red for Travel and green for Insurance in a finance report, where readers may take them as bad and good.
- The nine 2–4% slices are named only by matching their colour to the legend.
- Adjacent small slices are similar in lightness (blue/purple, teal/olive), so the pie would mostly lose its structure in greyscale.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The page holds back on colour: a warm off-white ground, near-black serif title, grey metadata, and one muted brown on the "4.2 COSTS" eyebrow (about 64,88). The chart is the only saturated thing on the page, so it gets all the attention.
- The value structure is clear. The title, subtitle, header and source line separate by lightness alone and would read the same in greyscale.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. There are no photos, illustrations, icons or logos on the page. The only visual is the pie chart, which belongs to the data section. "Harrowgate Instruments" at the top left (about x 64–236, y 29) is set in plain bold UI type, so it reads as a running head, not a logo.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies. There is one pie chart of 14 cost categories, with a value legend beside it.

**Findings**
1. **Does each chart use the form that fits its data and question?** The pie at x≈115–515, y≈235–630 has 14 slices. Nine of them are 1–4% slivers packed into the top-left quarter (x≈115–315, y≈235–435). The viewer reads the big four (38/16/12/9) right away. After that the slices become a fan of thin wedges whose angles can't be told apart: 4% vs 3% vs 2% looks the same, and you can only read the order from the small printed numbers. The chart itself does almost no comparing past the fourth slice, so it is a decorated version of the legend table. Few ("Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 5) and Wilke (*Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, ch. 10.1) limit pies to about five slices, and this matches the far end of that entry's range ("9 to 14 slices, four or more of them thin slivers"). Fix: keep the four or five largest slices and group the rest into one "Other (10 categories), 24%" slice, with the breakdown in the table. Or show all 14 as a sorted horizontal bar chart, which can absorb the legend. **Convention, major.**
2. **Is each series label placed at its data rather than in a separate legend? / Can each chart's series be told apart without colour vision?** (one problem) The slices carry only percentages. Every category name is in the legend at x≈620–1060, linked to its slice only by a swatch of about 12 px. To learn what the 3% sliver at about (150, 310) is, the reader has to find the yellow swatch in the legend and then work out which 3% it means, because four categories are 3% and four are 2%. Several hues are close: the dark blue Salaries, mid blue Software licences and indigo Utilities; the teal Rent and pale teal Equipment repair; the green Insurance and olive Bank fees. Red Travel sits next to green Insurance. A reader with a colour-vision deficiency can't reliably match the small slices to names at all, and everyone else has to look back and forth. Sources: Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, labels on the graphic; WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color. Fix: put the names on the data. With the "Other" grouping from finding 1, the four or five remaining slices can carry name plus % inside or beside the slice. With bars, the name sits at each bar and colour is no longer needed. **Defect, major.**
3. **Does each chart use few distinct colours for its series or categories, with grey for context?** There are 14 different saturated hues for one series of categories, and nothing points to any of them. Every colour is equally loud, so nothing is emphasised, and the palette is what forces the legend-matching in finding 2. Few (pitfall 12) and Wilke (ch. 19.1): use one colour for the series and keep a second for the one point the reader must notice. Fix: once the small categories are grouped, give the 4–5 named slices distinct hues and make "Other" grey. As bars, draw them all in one colour and accent Salaries if that is the point. **Convention, minor** (most of its cost is already counted in finding 2).
4. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** The title "Where operating costs went in fiscal 2026" (y≈123) and the subtitle name the topic, not the finding. The reader has to work out the message, which is probably "salaries are over a third of costs, and the top four take three quarters", from the wedges. The catalog's source here is off the approved list, so this is common sense: an annual-report reader skimming the page should get the point from the headline alone. Fix: make the title or subtitle the finding, e.g. "Salaries took 38% of operating costs; the top four categories, 75%". **Taste, minor.**

**What's working.**
- The shares are honest and in order. They add up to 100. The slices run clockwise from 12 o'clock in descending order, and the legend lists them in the same order. The source line states that figures are rounded, so the reader can trust the numbers they do find.
- It is flat and plain. There is no 3D, shadow, or exploded slice. The thin white slice borders and the light row rules in the legend leave nearly all the ink as data.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 12 yes, 4 no (chart form fits data; colour-vision-safe series; few colours; direct labels instead of legend), and the title-states-finding line is reported above as a no as well. Corrected tally: 16 lines, 11 yes, 5 no (chart form fits data; series told apart without colour; few distinct colours; labels at the data; title states the finding).

**Section.** Interface: skipped. This is a static annual-report page with one pie chart and its legend, and it has no buttons, links, fields, menus or navigation. The header line "Annual report 2026 · Section 4 of 9" is a running head that shows where you are in the report. It is not a control.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Interface: skipped
